canonical_statement: The study aimed to develop and validate machine-learning models that predict aPTT within 12 hours after a specified UFH bolus and maintenance dose.
The retrospective cohort comprised 3019 episodes of care from January 2017 through August 2020 across 5 hospitals in Queensland, Australia.

population.label: UFH-treated adult inpatient episodes across 5 Queensland hospitals

canonical_statement: Data from 4 hospitals were used for model development and cross-validation, while data from a fifth hospital were reserved for external validation.
Two prediction tasks were defined: regression of the numeric aPTT and multiclass classification as subtherapeutic (<70 s), therapeutic (70-100 s), or supratherapeutic (>100 s).
Modeling used H2O Driverless AI, and 17 experiments were iteratively conducted to optimize model accuracy.
Eligible episodes were adults who received a UFH bolus plus maintenance infusion for more than 48 hours, had a documented power plan, and had an aPTT recorded within 12 hours of the bolus.

population.label: Adults considered for the UFH modeling cohort
inclusion_criteria: aPTT within 12 hours after UFH bolus

canonical_statement: ICU patients were excluded because the ICU-specific EHR was not linked or integrated with the general EHR used for the study.
The 4 development hospitals contributed 2783 admissions involving 2470 patients.

population.label: Admissions identified at the 4 model-development hospitals

canonical_statement: The external-validation hospital contributed 236 admissions involving 221 patients.

population.label: Admissions identified at the external-validation hospital

canonical_statement: The investigators initially identified 15 EHR data tables for candidate feature extraction, intentionally using an inclusive set before later exclusions and feature engineering.
A UFH bolus was included only if it was a de novo first dose or followed at least 6 hours after prior UFH therapy cessation.
The first aPTT result was considered invalid if it was recorded more than 12 hours after the UFH bolus.
UFH maintenance infusions were considered invalid if not administered or if the infusion had been completed, stopped, or paused for more than 1 hour before aPTT testing.
After UFH/aPTT blending and filtering, the model-development data set contained 2158 records and the external-validation data set contained 236 records.
Three candidate EHR tables were excluded because each contained fewer than 278 of 2783 records (9.98%).
Missing baseline aPTT values, or values obtained more than 24 hours before the UFH bolus, were imputed to 30 seconds; corresponding baseline-aPTT timing was imputed to 1440 minutes.

source_anchor.table_row: Baseline aPTT and baseline aPTT minutes

canonical_statement: Missing weight and height were imputed to cohort averages after grouping by age, marital status, and sex.
Missing or older-than-12-hour vital-sign features were imputed using centroid values from k-means clustering with k=10.
Missing or older-than-1-week pathology results were imputed using centroid values from k-means clustering with k=10.
Missing or older-than-1-week Waterlow score and activities-of-daily-living values were imputed to 0.
Target aPTT values were bounded at 30 and 150 seconds to reduce the impact of a right-skewed distribution and outliers on regression modeling.
Cumulative UFH maintenance dose was calculated from syringe size and total infusion period multiplied by infusion time minus infusion-stop time.
A body-size feature was calculated as weight divided by height.
A UFH-bolus-time feature was calculated as UFH bolus dose divided by time to the target aPTT.
A combined UFH-bolus-time-and-size feature was calculated as body size multiplied by UFH bolus time.
Cosine cyclical transformations generated features for aPTT day of week, hour of day, and month of year.
Feature engineering produced 93 features in the aPTT fact table.
Continuous features were transformed using either Yeo-Johnson or min-max scaling according to their distributions.
Among 2783 training-data records, 1898 (68.2%) were male and 885 (31.8%) were female.
Among 2783 training-data records, 818 (29.4%) were categorized as acute coronary syndrome and 540 (19.4%) as venous thromboembolism.
The mean age in the training data set was 65.8 years (SD 14.6).
The mean body weight in the training data set was 87.8 kg (SD 26.7).
Mean baseline aPTT was 36 seconds (SD 11.1) in the training data set.
Mean UFH bolus dose was 4713 units (SD 1467) in the training data set.
Mean UFH maintenance amount was 6767 units (SD 4993) in the training data set.
Mean time between the UFH bolus and target aPTT was 364.1 minutes (SD 149).

source_anchor.table_row: Time between UFH bolus and aPTT

canonical_statement: Models were evaluated with 3-fold cross-validation using 67/33 splits, repeated 3 times, and iteration metrics were averaged.
For regression, 1126 alternative models were trained; feature evolution converted 93 original features to 188 features before model selection.
For multiclassification, 457 models were trained and tested, and evolved plus original features totaled 2196 features.
External validation used 236 records from Gold Coast University Hospital; a cited sample-size method yielded a minimum requirement of at least 235 participants.

The final multiclassification ensemble was a linear blend of four models: two XGBoost models and two LightGBM models.
The final H2O Driverless AI multiclassification ensemble achieved accuracy 0.599 in the reported model-development evaluation.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that the auto-ML regression and multiclassification models showed consistent performance when applied to an external data set from a fifth hospital.
The authors proposed a feasibility study integrating the model into hospital workflows, followed by evaluation of clinical utility against current standard practice if feasible.
The model was developed and validated within EHR data from 5 hospitals and should be tested in other health care systems.
The modeling approach applies to adult general medical and surgical inpatients and excluded ICU patients.
The model predicts aPTT after prespecified UFH bolus and maintenance doses; further work is required before it can calculate or adjust UFH doses.
Some model features, including activities-of-daily-living assessments, may not always be available at the time UFH is dosed.
Differences in EHR data standardization, measurement methods, aPTT assays, and data locations may affect model performance and generalizability.
UFH response is affected by many hematological and physiological factors that may be unmeasured or unknown, limiting achievable predictive performance.
